name: Qasr Al Hosn
funding: The pages read did not state a budget or the cost of the restoration. The National (25 October 2018) named the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi as the body behind the reopening, with its chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak speaking for it.
watch: Abu Dhabi's oldest building, an inner fort from around 1795 with an outer palace of 1939, reopened on 7 December 2018 after about a decade closed, together with the Cultural Foundation established by Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan in 1981. The Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi leads it.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: The fort and palace complex in central Abu Dhabi, with the Cultural Foundation building beside it (The National, 25 October 2018).

The inner fort dates to around 1795 and the outer palace to 1939; the Cultural Foundation was established by Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan in 1981; the site closed for renovation in 2008 and reopened on 7 December 2018 (The National, 25 October 2018).

What is there: archival material, interactive audio-visual displays and archaeological objects tracing Abu Dhabi from fishing and pearl diving to a modern city (The National, 25 October 2018); no object count was given. The site also runs the House of Artisans craft workshops (museum website).

Archive: the Cultural Foundation was planned with a Visual Arts Centre and a three-floor children's library (The National, 25 October 2018); the pages read did not describe an archive open to researchers.
details.funding_verdict: Qasr Al Hosn: public, run by Abu Dhabi's Department of Culture and Tourism; no amounts found.
funding: Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi: leads the reopening; its chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak said Qasr Al Hosn 'retraces the history of the city of Abu Dhabi, our very first building' (The National, 25 October 2018).
No reporting found, in the pages read, of the restoration cost or annual budget.
details.bottom_line: The pages read show a state-led heritage site with no amounts published. Nothing contested was found in them.

name: Sharjah Art Foundation
funding: Its parent organization is the Department of Culture and Information, Government of Sharjah.
watch: In April 2011 the foundation removed Maportaliche/It Has No Importance from the Sharjah Biennial. Director Jack Persekian was dismissed that month.
why_flagged: Its parent is a Government of Sharjah department and its president is the ruler's daughter, Hoor Al Qasimi. In April 2011 it removed a work and dismissed its director.
highlight: A contemporary art and cultural foundation in Sharjah, founded in 2009, which has managed the Sharjah Biennial since its creation.

overview: Contemporary art foundation in Sharjah with its Information Centre at Al Mureijah Square (SAF website).
Founded in 2009 by Hoor Al Qasimi, daughter of Sultan bin Muhammad Al-Qasimi, ruler of Sharjah. Wikipedia places it under the Department of Culture and Information, Government of Sharjah.
It took over the Sharjah Biennial, first held in 1993 under the Department of Culture and Information, in 2009 (Wikipedia).
Programmes: the Biennial, the March Meeting, residencies, grants, commissions and publications (SAF website, Wikipedia).
Visiting: Saturday to Thursday 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., Friday 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Most exhibitions and events are free. Free guided tours (SAF website).
details.funding_verdict: Sharjah Art Foundation: state-backed: the Sharjah ruler and Sharjah's government; no accounts published
funding: Ghalya Saadawi wrote in e-flux Journal (June 2011) that the Foundation is funded by the ruler and Sharjah's Ministry of Culture.
Her profile on the Foundation's site calls it "the independent public arts organisation she established in 2009" (SAF website).

red_flags.heading: Gulf state body
points: Wikipedia lists the Department of Culture and Information, Government of Sharjah, as parent organisation; Saadawi says the ruler and Sharjah's Ministry of Culture fund it. Hoor Al Qasimi, the ruler's daughter, is President and Director (SAF website).

red_flags.heading: State censorship and dismissal, 2011
points: On 6 April 2011 the ruler of Sharjah, Sheikh Sultan bin Mohammad Al Qasimi, dismissed director Jack Persekian without notice, after the 10th Sharjah Biennial opened on 16 March 2011 and public outcry over Mustapha Benfodil's installation "Maportaliche" (Sharjah Call for Action, e-flux; Jadaliyya).

The work was removed. Saadawi writes that other works were tampered with or placed "under review" (e-flux Journal); an audio piece was adjusted so it did not coincide with the call to prayer (ArtAsiaPacific, 18 April 2011).

Hoor Al Qasimi said the work paired sexually explicit language with religious references "in an overt and provocative manner" (Jadaliyya); ArtAsiaPacific reports the work was dismantled after "the public took enormous offense".

The Foundation said the online campaign was "deliberately misinforming the public" and that no staff had resigned (spokeswoman Sara Fitzmaurice, The National, 13 April 2011). The petition, with 1,627 signatures by Jadaliyya's 2 May 2011 report, demanded public acknowledgment of the censorship and threatened a boycott of the Biennial, the Foundation and Sharjah's cultural activities.

press.overall: Substantial criticism, almost all about the 2011 dismissal and censorship.

items.title: Ghalya Saadawi, "Post-Sharjah Biennial 10: Institutional Grease and Institutional Critique" (2011)
points: Says the ruler decided to remove Persekian and that the Foundation and its PR firm ran a campaign defending the decision.
Argues that large institutions everywhere depend on state, private or capital interests; calls for a renewed critique of institutions, not only moral condemnation.

items.title: unsigned news item, "Director's Ouster Jeopardizes Sharjah Art Foundation's Future" (2011)
points: Argues the dismissal threatens the Foundation and Biennial as regional platforms and risks self-censorship.
Quotes curators Rasha Salti and Haig Aivazian: "To shock was never our strategy, and offense never our intention."

items.title: author not named, "Boat Rocking in the Art Islands: Politics, Plots and Dismissals in Sharjah's Tenth Biennial" (2011)
points: Presents the dismissal as the decision of the ruler, Sheikh Sultan, and questions the international art world's ties to the UAE. The Foundation's reply is quoted.

items.outlet: Sharjah Call for Action, posted on e-flux
items.title: "An unwarranted dismissal in Sharjah" (2011)
points: Open letter, not an essay, published 11 April 2011: names the ruler as the one who dismissed Persekian on 6 April, calls the decision disproportionate, and threatens a boycott if its demands are not met.

wider_context: On 11 May 2015 Gulf Labor member Walid Raad was turned back at Dubai airport on his way to the Foundation's March Meeting; Gulf Labor campaigns for migrant workers on Abu Dhabi's Saadiyat Island. More than 40 artists in Sharjah Biennial 12 backed the banned artists (The Art Newspaper, Javier Pes, 1 June 2015).
The link to the Foundation is that the trip was to its event.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the Foundation is the ruler's and the state's, with no accounts or funder list published. The documented weak point is 2011, when the ruler dismissed the director over an artwork and other works were altered or placed under review; the Foundation disputed the petition. Watch for any published accounts or governance changes.

name: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilization
funding: The pages read did not state who funds it. Khaleej Times (9 June 2008) said it was opened by Sheikh Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah, as part of the Sharjah Museums Department's plan.
watch: A museum of over 5,000 objects in seven galleries, in a converted early 20th-century souq on the Sharjah corniche, opened in June 2008 by the Ruler of Sharjah. It is part of the Sharjah Museums Department's plan.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A museum in the former Souq Al Majarrah on the Sharjah corniche, with a dome mosaic of the night sky (Khaleej Times, 9 June 2008; The National, 24 July 2026).
Opened by Sheikh Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah, in June 2008; Manal Ataya was director of the Sharjah Museums Department (Khaleej Times, 9 June 2008).

What is there: more than 5,000 objects spanning 1,400 years in seven galleries, including Quran manuscripts, astrolabes, surgical instruments, celestial globes, ceramics, textiles, metalwork, musical instruments, coins and a section of the Kiswah from the Kaaba (The National, 24 July 2026). A loan show from the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin ran at opening (Khaleej Times, 9 June 2008).
Archive: the pages read did not mention a library or archive.
details.funding_verdict: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilization: public, Sharjah government; no amounts found.
funding: Sharjah Museums Department, headed in 2008 by Manal Ataya, ran the opening; Sheikh Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi opened it (Khaleej Times, 9 June 2008).
The pages read did not state a budget or operator today.
details.bottom_line: A ruler-opened state museum; the pages read give no funding figures.

name: Barbican Centre
funding: The City of London Corporation owns, funds and manages the Barbican Centre.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.

overview: Arts centre inside the Barbican Estate in the City of London, with a concert hall, theatre, art gallery, cinemas, library, conservatory, restaurants and conference halls (Wikipedia).

Built as the City of London's gift to the nation at a cost of £161 million. Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 3 March 1982 (Wikipedia). Wikipedia says the City of London Corporation owns, funds and manages it.
Building: designed by Chamberlin, Powell and Bon in the Brutalist style, listed Grade II in September 2001 (Wikipedia).
Venues: Barbican Hall (1,943 seats, home to the London Symphony Orchestra), Barbican Theatre (1,156 seats), The Pit (200 seats), Barbican Art Gallery, The Curve and three cinema screens (Wikipedia).
Visiting: the Barbican site has a "Free things to do" section and an Access Scheme.
details.funding_verdict: Barbican Centre: mainly public: the City of London Corporation
funding: The Barbican site calls the City of London Corporation "the founder and principal funder of the Barbican Centre".

In December 2024 the Corporation's Court of Common Council approved a £191 million package for repairs and upgrades, about 80% of the amount needed for the first phase of a five-year renewal programme, with a fundraising campaign launching in 2025 for the rest (International Arts Manager).

red_flags.heading: Protest and withdrawals over a cancelled Gaza lecture, 2024
points: February 2024: the Barbican decided not to host the London Review of Books lecture "The Shoah after Gaza" by Pankaj Mishra; the Guardian reported the cancellation on 6 February (Censorship at the Barbican campaign page). The Barbican said the lecture was publicised "prematurely" (Hyperallergic). The lecture took place at St James's Church, Clerkenwell, on 28 February (campaign page).

The collectors Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad Mayet withdrew two Loretta Pettway quilts from the "Unravel: The Power and Politics of Textiles in Art" exhibition, and the Barbican removed them on 29 February. Yto Barrada (7 March), Cian Dayrit and Diedrick Brackens (8 March), Mounira al Solh (9 March) and Art Jameel, which rescinded its loan of a Pacita Abad painting (11 March), followed; nine works in total (campaign page, run by Leviste and Mayet, an advocacy source).

The Barbican wrote on 22 February that "there was no intention to censor the speaker involved" (campaign page). It pointed to its 2023 Equity, Diversity & Inclusion Strategy and its London Palestine Film Festival, and put labels in the show stating that works were withdrawn "as an act of solidarity with Palestine" (Hyperallergic, campaign page).

press.overall: Three pieces cover the 2024 lecture cancellation and lender withdrawals, a 2021 book of staff accounts of racism, and a 2026 open letter over a director's departure.

items.title: Maya Pontone, "Lenders Withdraw Works From Barbican Show, Alleging 'Censorship'" (5 March 2024)
points: Reports that Leviste and Mayet withdrew two Pettway quilts on 29 February after the Barbican decided not to host the Mishra lecture.
Quotes Leviste calling the decision a "blatant act of repression" and the precedent "chilling".

items.title: Gareth Harris, "London's Barbican shakes up staff following racism allegations published in tell-all book" (10 August 2021)
points: Reports that "Barbican Stories", published in June 2021 by the Barbican Stories Collective, collects more than 100 accounts from current and former staff of discrimination dating back to 2014, describing the work culture as "subtle and insidiously" racist.

Reports that managing director Nicholas Kenyon was stepping down and that the City of London Corporation commissioned an external review of staff experiences of racism by the law firm Lewis Silkin LLP. Kenyon welcomed the review.

items.title: "Cultural figures sign open letter over departure of Barbican arts director" (20 February 2026, no author named)
points: Over 170 signatories, among them John Akomfrah, Isaac Julien, Salman Rushdie and Pankaj Mishra, asked the Barbican Board and the City of London Corporation to explain the departure of Devyani Saltzman, director for arts and participation, whose time in post the article calls "comparatively short".

The letter argues the departure raises questions about the institution's commitment to "global majority leadership at the highest levels" and asks the Barbican to publish current diversity data on senior leadership and commission an independent review of how senior appointments and exits are decided.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the Barbican is public: the City of London Corporation funds and runs it, with a £191 million renewal package approved in December 2024. In 2024 lenders and artists withdrew nine works in protest at the Barbican's decision not to host a Pankaj Mishra lecture, and press has covered a 2021 book of staff accounts of racism and a 2026 open letter over a director's departure.

name: Wellcome Collection
funding: Part of Wellcome, a charitable foundation. Wellcome's endowment was worth £29bn in July 2021, invested in shares, hedge funds, private equity and property.
watch: Wellcome faced a divestment call in March 2015 over fossil-fuel holdings and sold its BP and Shell shares in 2022.
why_flagged: Wellcome faced a divestment call in March 2015 over fossil-fuel holdings and sold its BP and Shell shares in 2022.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: No records of its own; its parent Wellcome Trust publishes annual reports and accounts 2019 to 2025 and its governors.
affiliations_note: Wellcome Collection is part of Wellcome, the charitable foundation, and has a long-term loan agreement with the Science Museum Group covering Sir Henry Wellcome's Museum Collection. Listed in the Art Fund directory.

overview: Free museum and library at 183 Euston Road, London.
Opened to the public in June 2007 and is part of the Wellcome Trust (Wikipedia). It follows an earlier Wellcome Historical Medical Museum at 54a Wigmore Street (Wikipedia).
Named for Sir Henry Wellcome (1853 to 1936, Wikipedia), whose will created the Wellcome Trust and left it his pharmaceutical company and his collection of historical medical items (Wellcome Trust).

Building: the Trust moved its administrative offices into the new Gibbs Building, designed by Michael Hopkins and Partners and completed in 2004. The Collection reopened with additional public spaces in October 2015 after a £17.5 million refurbishment, a transformation by Wilkinson Eyre (Wikipedia).
On site: galleries, a library, a café and a shop. The collection holds rare books, artworks, films and videos, personal archives and objects on health and medicine (stated by the museum).

Visiting: exhibitions, events and library access are free. Galleries are open 10:00 to 18:00 and the library 10:00 to 16:00 on the day checked. Step-free access and hearing loops are provided, and BSL-interpreted and Deaf-led BSL tours run for major exhibitions (stated by the museum).
details.funding_verdict: Wellcome Collection: endowed: the Wellcome Trust's investment portfolio, about £38 billion
funding: The Trust says it is not funded by GSK or any other pharmaceutical company and pays for its work from its investment portfolio, worth around £38 billion (Wellcome Trust).
The endowment began with Henry Wellcome's will in 1936, which left the Trust his pharmaceutical company. Wellcome plc was sold to Glaxo from 1995 (Wellcome Trust).

red_flags.heading: Wellcome Trust fossil-fuel investments
points: Campaign: on 19 March 2015 The Guardian launched a petition, signed by more than 93,000 people, asking the Wellcome Trust and the Gates Foundation to divest from the top 200 fossil fuel companies within five years and to freeze new investments in them (Civil Society).
Holdings in 2015: Civil Society reported that the Trust's direct equity holdings included Shell and BP, together worth £260 million. It gave no share of the endowment.

Response: the Trust called climate change "one of the greatest contemporary challenges facing our society" and "highly complex", and said it engaged with policymakers, researchers and the businesses it invests in (Civil Society, 2015).

Sale: in 2022 Wellcome sold its BP and Shell shares, saying it was concentrating its holdings in "non-cyclical industries" and that the sales were "not a reflection of the companies' approach to the energy transition" (Civil Society, 21 July 2022).
The campaign targeted the Trust, not the museum.

press.overall: Criticism of the Collection exists but sits mostly in general-press and academic pieces, not specialist art outlets. It comes from two opposite sides: that the Collection did too little to confront Wellcome's colonial collecting, and that it distances itself too far from its founder.

items.title: Anaïs Walsdorf, "Why Wellcome closed its Medicine Man exhibition, and others should follow suit" (2022)
points: Argues the gallery told history from a narrow Eurocentric view centred on Henry Wellcome, with little context on how objects were acquired, and that museums should go beyond adding perspectives to displays.
Says a summer 2022 report found that Wellcome perpetuated "systematic racism" and described discrimination faced by staff.
The author is a former Wellcome Collection employee.

items.title: Ross Clark, "What has become of the Wellcome Collection?" (2024)
points: Argues the Hard Graft exhibition is multimedia art, not the scholarly show the Collection once staged.
Criticises the Collection for distancing itself from its founder, whom he says it dismisses as an "evil colonialist".
An opinion-driven arts review in the 5 October 2024 magazine issue.

wider_context: The Guardian's 2015 petition and the 2022 sale of BP and Shell shares concern the Trust's investments, not the museum.
The Collection is part of the Trust and is paid for from the same endowment.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the Collection is the Wellcome Trust's single endowment, built on a pharmaceutical firm and no named outside donor. The weak points are the Trust's fossil-fuel holdings, which drew a documented 2015 campaign and included BP and Shell shares sold in 2022, and the Collection's colonial-era acquisitions. Worth watching: the Trust's remaining fossil fuel investments, which no page opened states.

name: Albuquerque Museum
funding: A division of the City of Albuquerque's Department of Arts and Culture. The pages read did not state its budget; the Albuquerque Museum Foundation Inc is listed as a separate nonprofit filer.
watch: Established in 1967 in Old Town as a city museum of art, history and culture, with about 10,000 works of art and 35,000 historical objects.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: A separate Albuquerque Museum Foundation Inc files as EIN 85-0201054 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer search).

overview: Albuquerque Museum, 2000 Mountain Road NW, Old Town, a division of the City of Albuquerque's Department of Arts and Culture (city website).
Established in 1967 (city website).
What is there: roughly 10,000 works of art and 35,000 historical objects (city website).
Archive: more than 130,000 items in its photo archives, searchable through the e-Museum (city website).
details.funding_verdict: Albuquerque Museum: a city department museum, foundation support not detailed in the pages read
funding: The museum is a division of the City of Albuquerque's Department of Arts and Culture (city website).
No reporting found in the pages read of the city appropriation, foundation grants or sponsors.
details.bottom_line: A city-run museum, so public money pays for it; the amounts and the foundation's role are not in the pages read. No controversy was found.

name: Crow Museum of Asian Art
funding: Founded and paid for by Trammell and Margaret Crow; the Crow family gave the whole collection to The University of Texas at Dallas in 2019. The pages read named no other funders and gave no amounts.
watch: Opened in December 1998 as a free museum in the Dallas Arts District; since the 2019 gift it is part of UT Dallas, with a second site at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum in Richardson.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Crow Museum of Asian Art, 2010 Flora Street, Dallas Arts District, and a second site at 800 W. Campbell Road, Richardson, on the UT Dallas campus (museum website).
The Crows opened the museum as a free, permanent museum in December 1998; the collection grew from their first Asian art purchase in the mid-1960s (museum website, History page).

What is there: art of China, Japan, India, Korea and Southeast Asia, bought mostly through private dealers, auction houses and major collections such as the Morrie A. Moss collection; Asian art expert Clarence Shangraw selected 569 pieces for the permanent collection. The page gives no current total (museum website).

In 2019 the Crow family donated the entire collection to The University of Texas at Dallas; UT Dallas opened Phase I of the Athenaeum in 2024 (museum website, History page). The pages read do not describe an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Crow Museum of Asian Art: family gift to a state university
funding: Trammell and Margaret Crow founded the museum and built the collection; the Crow family donated it to UT Dallas in 2019, in memory of their parents (museum website, History page).
The pages read named no other funders and gave no budget; no Form 990 under the museum's name was found in ProPublica search.
details.bottom_line: A family collection now held by a public university; the money after 2019 is UT Dallas and any donors the pages read do not name. No controversy was found.

name: Folger Shakespeare Library
funding: The pages read did not state the Library's funders or amounts; its site says its Board of Governors operates under the auspices of Amherst College and invites donations, memberships and planned giving.
watch: A research library and theatre on Capitol Hill founded by Henry Clay Folger and Emily Folger, opened in 1932 and governed by a Board of Governors under Amherst College's auspices. Its site says it holds more than 300,000 objects.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Its site refers to an Annual Report with financial statements; no Form 990 was found under its name on ProPublica.

overview: The Folger Shakespeare Library is a library, museum and theatre at 201 East Capitol Street SE in Washington (Folger website).

It opened in 1932 as a gift to the American people from Henry and Emily Folger, who made their first rare book purchase in 1889; its Board of Governors operates under the auspices of Amherst College, Henry Clay Folger's alma mater (Folger website).

What is there: more than 300,000 objects, including rare books, manuscripts and works of art from the early modern period; the site calls it the world's largest Shakespeare collection (Folger website).

Archive: the collection is available in the Reading Room to anyone researching Shakespeare or the early modern world, with researcher registration, reference services and an online catalogue (Folger website).
details.funding_verdict: Folger Shakespeare Library: funders not stated in the pages read; governed by a board under Amherst College's auspices
funding: The Folger's site invites donations, memberships and planned giving and mentions an Annual Report with financial statements; the pages read did not give amounts (Folger website).
No Form 990 was found under the Folger's name on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, so no revenue figures are stated here.
details.bottom_line: The Folger's own pages name no funder or budget, and no independent account was read. Its legal link to Amherst College is the thing to follow. Look for the Annual Report it mentions.

name: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth
funding: 2025-26 grants include Sid W. Richardson Foundation, Ben E. Keith Foundation, Bank of America Charitable Foundation, City of Fort Worth and Texas Commission on the Arts.
watch: Sid W. Richardson's oil fortune funds its foundation, which gave in 2025-26. Fort Worth police seized Sally Mann photographs in January 2025; no charges followed.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: Form 990 filings for 2001 to 2025 sit on ProPublica.
finances_note: FY2024-25 income USD 21.0M: no government grants on line 1e, about 50 percent donations and gifts, 4 percent earned, 45 percent investment income (Form 990).
affiliations_note: Accredited by the American Alliance of Museums. It sits in the Cultural District near the Kimbell and Amon Carter, with no formal partnership stated. Member of AAMD.

overview: Museum of international modern and contemporary art in the Cultural District of Fort Worth, Texas, known as The Modern (Wikipedia).
First chartered in 1892 as the Fort Worth Public Library and Art Gallery. Later names included Fort Worth Art Museum, Fort Worth Art Center and Fort Worth Museum of Art (Wikipedia).
Current building designed by the Japanese architect Tadao Ando, opened on 14 December 2002: three long pavilions set into a reflecting pond with about 53,000 square feet of gallery space (Wikipedia).
Collection of more than 3,000 works, mostly from 1945 onward, including Picasso, Pollock, Rothko and Warhol (Wikipedia).

Closed Mondays. Open 10 am to 5 pm, Friday until 8 pm. Admission is $16 for adults, $12 for seniors, military and first responders, $10 for students, free under 18. Fridays are free and Sundays half price. Free for up to four people with a SNAP EBT card. Galleries are closed 29 September to 30 October 2026 (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth: private foundations and local government: Texas foundations, bank foundations, the City of Fort Worth and the Texas Commission on the Arts
funding: The museum's Foundation Support page lists 21 funders under the heading "2025-2026 Grants" (donations of $250 or more): Arts Fort Worth, Bank of America Charitable Foundation, Ben E. Keith Foundation, CAF America, Bratton Family Foundation, City of Fort Worth, Crystelle Waggoner Charitable Trust (Bank of America trustee), Communities Foundation of Texas, DAFgiving360, Fash Foundation, Fidelity Charitable Gift Fund, Fort Worth Promotion and Development Fund, Fort Worth Tourism Public Improvement District, Jedel Family Foundation, John & Amy Griffin Foundation, North Texas Community Foundation, Raymond James Charitable, Sid W. Richardson Foundation, Terrell and Patsy Small Family Foundation, Texas Commission on the Arts and Three G Foundation.

Sid W. Richardson Foundation: set up in 1947 by Sid W. Richardson, who earned his fortune in the oil industry (Wikipedia). The foundation's own site says its grantmaking began in 1962, when income from assets of Richardson's estate became available. It had about $526.8 million in total assets in December 2024 and gave the Modern $750,000 for operational support in 2017 (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: Police seizure of Sally Mann photographs
points: The Fort Worth Police Department seized Sally Mann photographs from the exhibition "Diaries of Home" by 7 January 2025 (Cardinal News, Charles Paullin, 27 March 2025). The museum's statement referred to four works (The Art Newspaper, Elena Goukassian, 9 January 2025).

Complaint: The Art Newspaper reports that a complaint said the images show naked children and could be seen as pornographic, that a police report was filed against the museum and that the first story came from The Dallas Express on 23 December 2024. FIRE says several local officials complained in December 2024. A Tarrant County judge posted on X on 8 January 2025 urging police to investigate (Cardinal News).

Museum: a spokesperson said the photographs had been published and exhibited for more than 30 years in leading cultural institutions (The Art Newspaper). The museum's attorney, Michael Anderson, thanked the grand jury for its review (Cardinal News).

Outcome: a Tarrant County grand jury declined to take action against museum employees on 25 March 2025, and police said the photographs would be returned (Cardinal News); FIRE reports that police closed the case against Mann and the museum and returned the artwork in April 2025.
The National Coalition Against Censorship and Artists At Risk Connection condemned the seizure (The Art Newspaper).
Funding link: the museum's Foundation Support page lists the City of Fort Worth among its 2025-2026 funders; the Fort Worth Police Department made the seizure.

details.bottom_line: The museum's listed funders are Texas foundations, bank charitable foundations, donor-advised funds and city and state arts bodies. One of them, the Sid W. Richardson Foundation, was set up in 1947 by an oilman, and its own site dates its grantmaking from his estate's income in 1962. In January 2025 city police seized Sally Mann photographs from a museum exhibition; the grand jury declined to take action in March 2025, and the City of Fort Worth is a listed funder.

name: MoMA (The Museum of Modern Art)
funding: Admissions, individual board donations, UNIQLO.
watch: Leon Black still a trustee after Epstein payments; Fink, Crown and Dubin named in Strike MoMA and the 2024 sit-in.
why_flagged: Leon Black still a trustee after Epstein payments; Fink, Crown and Dubin named in Strike MoMA and the 2024 sit-in.
records_note: Its Year in Review reports run from 2014 to 2025, with audited statements and Form 990 posted; the donor list seen is dated 2016.
finances_note: FY2024-25 income USD 362.0M: no government grants reported, about 27 percent donations and memberships, 24 percent earned, 49 percent investment income (Form 990, Part VIII).
affiliations_note: MoMA PS1 states that it is affiliated with The Museum of Modern Art, an affiliation that began in 2000. Member of AAMD, CIMAM, Gallery Climate Coalition.

overview: Modern and contemporary art museum on West 53rd Street in Midtown Manhattan (Wikipedia).
Opened on 7 November 1929 at 730 Fifth Avenue, with A. Conger Goodyear as president and Alfred H. Barr Jr. as first director (Wikipedia).
Moved to its current building, designed by Philip L. Goodwin and Edward Durell Stone, in 1939. An expansion adding 47,000 square feet of galleries reopened on 21 October 2019 (Wikipedia).
Glenn Lowry directed it from 1995 and announced in September 2024 that he would step down in 2025 (Hyperallergic, 10 September 2024). Wikipedia lists Christophe Cherix as director.
Adult admission is USD 30. New York State residents enter free on Friday evenings, 17:30 to 20:30 (Uniqlo Friday Nights, Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: MoMA: private: admissions, trustees' gifts and endowment, with corporate partners
funding: MoMA is a private nonprofit that does not accept government funding; Wikipedia gives annual revenue of about USD 145 million (undated).
David Rockefeller gave USD 77 million in cash toward the 2002 to 2004 expansion and pledged USD 100 million to the endowment in 2005 (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: Leon Black, Epstein payments
points: Role: Black was MoMA board chair from 1 July 2018 to 1 July 2021 and remains a trustee (Wikipedia). He announced on 22 March 2021 that he was leaving the chair, citing health reasons (Hyperallergic, 23 March 2021).

Payments: The Art Newspaper (19 August 2025) reported that Black paid Epstein at least USD 158 million between 2012 and 2017 for tax and estate planning advice. CBS News (updated 4 June 2026) reported that Senator Ron Wyden wrote the total was USD 170 million for 2012 to 2017. These were payments from Black to Epstein, not to MoMA; neither article says any money went to the museum.

Wyden wrote that Black has not given a "credible explanation" (CBS News). Black's lawyers say a Dechert review found he paid Epstein for estate planning and tax advice only. MoMA did not respond to The Art Newspaper.
Unverified: Hyperallergic's newsletter (5 February 2026) reported allegations against Black in released Epstein files; he denies them.

red_flags.heading: Glenn Dubin, Epstein links
points: Role: Hyperallergic called Dubin a MoMA trustee in November 2019, September 2020 and January 2024; The Art Newspaper named him among five targeted trustees in March 2021.

Hyperallergic reported on 10 September 2020 that Epstein received USD 15 million for introducing Dubin to a JPMorgan Chase executive around Dubin's 2004 sale of Highbridge Capital, and invested in Dubin's hedge fund; US Virgin Islands subpoena notices were filed on 3 September 2020. A Dubin representative said the Dubins "categorically reject" the allegations.
Unverified: Virginia Giuffre testified that Ghislaine Maxwell told her to give Dubin a "massage"; Dubin has denied it (Hyperallergic, 4 January 2024).

red_flags.heading: Protests aimed at trustees and the museum
points: January 2020: 37 artists in the MoMA PS1 show "Theater of Operations" asked MoMA to divest from trustees whose money profits from others' suffering, naming Fink's BlackRock and Black's Apollo (Hyperallergic, 14 January 2020).
From 9 April 2021: Strike MoMA, a ten-week coalition action, targeted trustees Black, Steven Tananbaum, Dubin, Steven Cohen and Larry Fink (The Art Newspaper, 24 March 2021).

10 February 2024: more than 500 protesters occupied the atrium and MoMA closed its galleries; they named Black, Fink, Paula Crown, Marie-Josee Kravis and Ronald Lauder (Hyperallergic, 10 February 2024). Unverified: the protesters say these trustees fund genocide.

press.overall: Criticism targets trustees and their money, not programming; most is protest reporting.

items.title: Hakim Bishara, "Guerrilla Girls Target MoMA Trustees With Ties to Jeffrey Epstein in an Ad Takeover" (2019)
points: Asks MoMA to remove Black and Dubin from its board and drape galleries named for them in black.
Reports the Dubins' and the Black family's denials; no MoMA statement.

items.title: Hakim Bishara, "Artist Coalition Announces 10-week 'Strike' Against MoMA" (2021)
points: Argues MoMA itself and its reliance on billionaire donors are the problem, not only individual trustees. MoMA did not respond.

items.title: newsletter, no byline, "When Will MoMA Dump Leon Black?" (2026)
points: Argues MoMA should cut ties with Black after new allegations in released files; a newsletter digest.

details.bottom_line: MoMA's operating money is private, but its board is the weak point: Black, a trustee, paid Epstein at least USD 158 million (The Art Newspaper), and Hyperallergic reported business links between Dubin and Epstein. Worth watching: whether MoMA acts on Black's trusteeship.
